With edge 4 absent, removing edge 3 leaves only the edge-5 path to the output, so the network can nearly collapse (expt 68: -75 on C10).
When node 1 has no direct route to the output, deleting edge 5 cuts all deep computation from the output (expts 72,73 vs 71,74-76).
Without the edge-3 shortcut, edge 5 may be one of very few routes to the output, so removing it is much more damaging (expt 73).
If edge 1 is absent, removing edge 0 disconnects nodes 1 and 2 from the input entirely (expts 29,30: about -15 IN16 vs about -2 otherwise).
Adding a node1-to-output conv path helps more when the output lacks the direct edge-3 input (expt 38 vs 31,39).
A skip on edge 4 partially replaces the missing input-to-output residual, which gives large gains especially on ImageNet16 (expts 95,96 vs 91-94).
When edge 5 is absent, replacing the edge-4 conv with skip removes the main remaining deep path into the output (expt 97 vs 91).
In parameter-free pooling-heavy cells, the first conv on edge 0 adds most of the learnable capacity (expt 87: +48 C10 vs about +1 in conv-rich cells).
Adding a conv is far more valuable in conv-poor, skip-dominated cells than in cells already full of 3x3 convs (expt 60 vs 51-55).

I weighted the interactions that show up as large, consistent contrasts in the 100 measurements, and checked that each matches how information flows through the cell DAG:
- **Restoring connectivity:** an edit that reconnects a cut-off path helps much more than one that adds a redundant path. Examples are a skip on edge 3 when it is `none`, and conv or skip on edge 4 when edge 3 is `none`.
- **Cutting the last path:** an edit that removes the only remaining path to the output hurts much more. Example: removing edge 5 when edges 3 or 4 are already `none`.
- **Conv-poor parents:** adding a conv helps most when the parent has almost no convs, such as all-pool or all-skip cells.
